### Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The genealogy of the right to mental integrity does not originate in a legal vacuum, but rather from the protracted historical struggle of human civilization against novel forms of power seeking to penetrate its most private sanctuary: human consciousness itself. When international human rights instruments were formulated in the mid-20th century—amid the haunting shadows of totalitarian medical experiments, concentration camps, and Cold War psychological manipulation—architects of international law projected the physical body and domestic privacy as the primary bastions of individual freedom (Weizenbaum, 1976; Jonas, 1979). Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and Article 3 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union were historically interpreted through a narrow somatic lens: the absolute prohibition of physical torture, cruel, inhuman treatment, and unauthorized biomedical interventions (Floridi, 2013). However, the escalation of generative artificial intelligence technologies, persuasive technology architectures, commercial neuro-data mining, and digital environmental engineering has shattered these physical boundaries, radically altering the threat landscape (Zuboff, 2019; Farahany, 2023). The line demarcating the biological body from the cognitive space has blurred, demanding a profound epistemological re-reading—one that positions mental integrity not merely as a secondary derivative of the right to privacy, but as a standalone ontological entity serving as the foundation of human autonomy (Searle, 1980; Hildebrandt, 2015).

Epistemologically, the concept of mental integrity implies that the human mind, emotions, memory, and cognitive processes possess an inherent sovereignty that must never be reduced to mere data commodities, random variables, or fodder for multinational corporate behavioral prediction models (Wiener, 1950; Calo, 2014). In the contemporary digital era, where attention-mining algorithms map the latent space of our deepest fears, hidden desires, and psychological vulnerabilities, interventions are no longer physically coercive or visibly transparent. Instead, they permeate insidiously into the subconscious decision-making structures (Kahneman, 2011). If classical human rights instruments shielded individuals from the strike of a baton, solitary confinement, or the injection of chemical sedatives, cutting-edge threats manifest as neuro-ergonomically designed interface manipulations devised to neutralize free will without the victim's conscious awareness (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). Therefore, a reinterpretation of the ICCPR, the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), and other universal declarations is urgently required—not merely as an additive statutory amendment, but as a philosophical transformation acknowledging that assaults on an individual's cognitive structures constitute a violation of human dignity whose destructiveness far exceeds conventional physical violence (Husserl, 1913; Levinas, 1961).

This transformation demands a fundamental theoretical paradigm shift: from negative liberty (the classical freedom from arbitrary state intervention) toward cognitive sovereignty, wherein international and domestic law must be capable of protecting citizens from digital environmental engineering engineered to compromise mental autonomy (Dreyfus, 1972; Floridi, 2013). When algorithmic systems possess the capacity to predict, trigger, and exploit an individual's psychological vulnerabilities before the individual even registers those emotional fluctuations, conventional human rights protection instruments suffer from a severe conceptual paralysis (Turing, 1950; Weizenbaum, 1976). The antiquated doctrine of informed consent collapses instantly under the weight of manipulative designs that systematically exploit the cognitive biases of the human brain, such as confirmation bias, loss aversion, and hyperbolic discounting (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979, 1984; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).
